lines.text: Picture a transfer, mid-flight, when the power dies. Ten dollars already left account A. It never reached account B.
Four letters are supposed to be the reason that can't happen to you.
So let's actually say what each one promises, instead of just reciting the acronym.
First letter. I ran a real transfer against a real table, with a rule built in: two columns always have to sum to one hundred.
I deliberately let the second half of that transfer fail.
The row came back exactly as it started. Not half changed. Nothing at all.
Here's where I want you to actually commit to an answer before I give you mine.
The engine clearly does check some rules, since you just watched it enforce one.
So who really owns keeping the database correct: the engine, because it's the one doing the checking, or the application?
The trap is that the engine really does check rules, so it's tempting to hand it the whole job.
But it only checks the rules you actually wrote down. Anything you never declared, it has no way to know about.
So the honest answer is both, split: the engine owns what you told it, and the application owns everything you didn't.
I measured both halves of that split directly.
A rule I did declare, stock can't go negative, got blocked outright, no question.
A rule I never declared, reservations can't exceed what's on hand, slipped straight through. Fifty three reserved against ten on hand, committed without a single complaint.
Third letter. I ran the identical interleaving twice, once under each of two real isolation levels.
Under Read Committed, a transaction re-read the row and actually saw the other transaction's change land in the middle of its own work: one hundred, then one hundred ten.
Under Repeatable Read, the exact same interleaving, same code, and it never saw that change at all. One hundred, then one hundred, the whole way through.
Fourth letter. I watched what actually happens the instant a transaction commits.
The server's own write ahead log position measurably moved forward, right then.
And a brand new connection, one that had nothing to do with writing that data, read the committed value straight back.

tolerated.line: The server's own write ahead log position measurably moved forward, right then.

lines.text: One more thing before we pull this together, and it genuinely surprised me.
IBM's own IMS system was already running transactions with all four of these guarantees back in nineteen seventy three.
The acronym that actually names them didn't get coined until nineteen eighty three. A full decade of running it before anyone needed a word for it.
So, four letters, stated precisely instead of recited.
Atomicity: all or nothing, even mid crash. Isolation: as if you were the only one running. Durability: a commit survives everything after it.
And consistency, the one that isn't owned by just one side: the engine keeps its own promises, and the application has to keep the rest.
